content: Discussion thread for #Project announcements > A project on optimizing Lean
Very interesting --- thanks for sharing your findings! Great performance improvements are always great; the best build time is zero :-)

Let me share a few comments and questions:

  • mandatory question these days: did you use LLMs for some of the coding or writing? (It's nice to say if an LLM was used, so readers can adjust accordingly.)

  • "The use of Lean for mathematics now appears to account for the overwhelming majority of all Lean
    usage" seems quite false to me. It might be true on this Zulip, but that's only because this is not representative of the whole community. If anything, it*s becoming less true, because Lean is making big inroads into software verification.

  • these days, I'm not sure if lean-repl is really the tool of choice. I've seen lean-lsp-mcp become a de facto tool used.

  • these measurements are on MacOS X, right? (One of your changes is mac-only... so saying so early seems helpful.)
  • is change (2) changing the .olean file format, or am I misunderstanding? (That makes it interesting, but sadly also a bit harder to get merged...)
  • I believe @Sebastian Ullrich has done work optimizing refcount traffic in Lean core also. It would be nice to see how your changes compare.
  • aside: my main suggestion regarding improvement 5 is to not use exact? or apply? (which are not really maintained any more), but @Jovan Gerbscheid's #click_suggestions command. In my experience, this gives much better results also. This information is probably not as widely known yet, so let me share it here as a tip for everybody who wants to hear it :-)

Actually, regarding item (4): did you use the module system already? (Do you know what this is? No worries if not, but I don't want to 'splain you.) That trick will easily save a lot of memory and speed up importing.
If you haven't, I strongly suspect that this will be the proper way to reap these benefits.

Quick summary of the changes for the impatient

  1. address reservation (mac-only)
  2. change .olean file layout (if I understood correctly)
  3. optimize reference count traffic
  4. is similar to "use the module system"
  5. speed up exact? or apply? by pre-building its discrimination trees
  6. pre-build discrimination trees for simp (if I understood correctly)
  7. improving the built-in snapshot tool
  8. compile mathlib tactics
  9. crazy idea: can we fork a Lean process (e.g. having imported mathlib) once to optimize?

Thanks. Yes, I definitely used AI, pretty heavily, for developing the improvements and much else. For writing of the paper, the AI drafted writeups and that was my starting point, but the writing wasn't good, I rewrote 98% of it to make it understandable. The paper has an "acknowledgment of AI usage" section so I'm transparent about everything. (And I took care to write that I take responsibility not just for the contents but for the quality of the writing, because I personally do not enjoy reading a lot of the slop I run into these days.)

Do you have ablation data on the build time for a from scratch project? simp/general env extension setup time and compile mathlib tactics have been on my radar as well for a while. I didnt dare to do the serialization of simp trees because people already complain our install size is too big anyway. The big issue with using pre compile modules is that we have to distribute the cache to several platforms etc. so its mostly an engineering thing at this point until we get there . I'd be curious how much of the improvement on build time is made up by the remaining approach.

The measurements are not macOS only. I also did measurements on a Docker container running Linux, and on AWS Linux machines, both ARM-based and x86. The setup and the different machines are discussed in the paper. One of the improvements is macOS only (and yields pretty significant performance gains there) but the others should be useful on any architecture. Funnily enough, for the macOS-specific improvement, it has to do with what's called the Shlemiel the painter's algorithm, a well-known algorithm design fallacy that shows up here in some low-level details of how macOS allocates addresses. So maybe it's not a Lean problem but actually an OS-level issue. I have a plan to investigate this further at some point...

Michael, I'm aware of the module system and that many things should work better with it. I'm not sure how much of the benchmarking I did used modules, probably not very much. This project is my initial attempt to delve into the technicalities of the toolchain and see what opportunities for improvement exist. It wouldn't surprise me if it turns out that some of my ideas will be superseded by modules or other recent innovations, but I also expect some of these ideas are genuinely useful even with modules.

Michael: change (2) is not changing the file format. None of my changes do - that was a core requirement for developing the improvements that they should not change any formats and they should not change Lean's behavior. For improvement number 4, I discuss a possible version of it that would change file formats, which I didn't implement, and would have some advantages over the version I did build, which didn't change the format. That's at the end of section 3.4 in the paper.

re: module system
I'm asking because you're e.g. referencing "I can't import MIL with just 8GB of Ram", and that should disappear once MIL uses the module system. (I doesn't yet; there's an open PR about it, and the main blocking question is "how do you teach this to beginners without confusing or overwhelming them".)

Ah, found it in §3.4:

The older style of file — one that opens directly with import Mathlib and carries no module
declaration — still loads everything, and that is what nearly everyone writes today, including every file
in our corpus

In other words: improvement (4) needs no Lean changes --- just a change to "modulise" the project you're working on. :-)

Henrik: the data I have is described in the writeup and repo. (Admittedly it's not much, I didn't work that hard on doing the most extensive testing.) I can try to generate more ablation data if you give me more precise guidance on what you have in mind with "build time for a from scratch project".

I maintain the nixpkgs packages for leanclient and lean-lsp-mcp. Fair warning that I have been slow on them, since most of my time is going to Rocq at the moment. If anyone here uses either from nixpkgs and would like to co-maintain. Version bumps are mostly automated, so it is a light load, and it just needs someone around to look at the PRs.

Dan Romik said:

change (2) is not changing the file format. None of my changes do - that was a core requirement for developing the improvements that they should not change any formats and they should not change Lean's behavior.

Can you clarify what methodology you took to make sure this was the case, and that the AI wasn't sneakily changing Lean/Mathlib behavior without telling you about it?

Michael Rothgang said:

  1. crazy idea: can we fork a Lean processing (e.g. having imported mathlib) once to optimize?

This would be amazing! This is something I've wanted for a while (and I'm sure others too). As Dan's fork-safety.md explains, Lean uses multiple worker threads but a naive unix fork() only clones the main process but fails to copy all the threads. This makes fuzzing in Lean much slower than it probably needs to be.

Jack McCarthy said:

Can you clarify what methodology you took to make sure this was the case, and that the AI wasn't sneakily changing Lean/Mathlib behavior without telling you about it?

I looked at the code, and I also discussed it with the AI, and feel reasonably comfortable that my claims about what the code is doing are a faithful representation of what it's actually doing. I can't vouch for this with absolute certainty, and it's healthy to view this with skepticism. Obviously, none of this code should be incorporated into official Lean without a thorough review by humans.

Jack McCarthy said:

  1. crazy idea: can we fork a Lean processing (e.g. having imported mathlib) once to optimize?

This would be amazing! This is something I've wanted for a while (and I'm sure others two). As Dan's fork-safety.md explains, Lean uses multiple worker threads but a naive unix fork() only clones the main process but fails to copy all the threads. This makes fuzzing in Lean much slower than it probably needs to be.

Re: the crazy idea, I actually have additional and fairly substantial work that I didn't include in the current project about a "single import walker": a build process for large projects that would iterate over the build, using forking and incrementally importing modules in a path on the build tree that eliminates repetitive imports. My AI and I ran some tests that partially validated the idea, but it's an unfinished and very experimental setup, so I decided to leave it out for now and just ship the current set of improvements. There are many issues still with forking, it's not at all a simple problem to resolve. See the discussion in section 3.10. There are two open Zulip threads about it (referenced in the paper) and I'll be posting details there soon as well.

As a general note, even with challenges to upstream to lean, I'm very interested in strategies that can be applied (without changes to the toolchain) to accelerate a build even if they hold in a narrow circumstance or require some ad-hoc set-up. They might pose a challenge to upstream to Lean core as for that they need to 'generalize', as in the above

The big issue with using pre compile modules is that we have to distribute the cache to several platforms etc. so its mostly an engineering thing at this point until we get there .

but if they compose well with the existing toolchain, they can be of great improvement for faster CI / automation set-ups (e.g., mathlib PR validations), where the environment is controlled can be 'narrow' (in fact, we only ever build on Linux for Mathlib CI). In a way, mathlib's lake exe cache get can be viewed as exactly one of these strategies.

Dan Romik said:

Henrik: the data I have is described in the writeup and repo. (Admittedly it's not much, I didn't work that hard on doing the most extensive testing.) I can try to generate more ablation data if you give me more precise guidance on what you have in mind with "build time for a from scratch project".

One of your benchmarks mentions compiling a project from scratch right?

Re: the proposed change to exact?: in fact, in the past we used to ship a prepared discrimination tree, but removed it in part because it was too big. (It also predated the lazy construction of the discrimination tree, without which it was basically necessary.)

We're already quite concerned about cache serving costs, so my initial impression is that we are unlikely to ship this. Particularly given the declining usefulness of exact? (e.g. Jovan's #click_suggestions alternative, and the fact that AIs just find these things themselves without much difficulty).

But I'd be happy to have (informed, expert users only please) feedback on whats users would prefer (absolutely no promises, there's also a financial decision about cache serving here!).
/poll Would you (expert Mathlib user!) prefer
Could it also speed-up try?? That would be a better win, since it takes ~10s every time, and we now have autoTry
If the downside is just about storage, is there a world where this can be parameterized? Or even having these supporting data structures for "optimization" in an optional sideband file?

In other words: improvement (4) needs no Lean changes --- just a change to "modulise" the project you're working on. :-)

I think this deserves to be more widely advertised. "modulising" the project doesn't need to mean minimising dependencies, simply adding module at the top in a single file project while continuing to import "all of mathlib" speeds things up by 0.5s and reduced memory consumption by 2.4GB on my test. The "post-modulised" thing I used for tests is

module
import Mathlib

example (x y : ℝ) (h : x < y) : (x + y) / 2 < y := by
  linarith
